title: £1,000 Into Your Pension for Just £720? The Payslip Trick Most People Miss 😮💷 #shorts
description:
£1,000 into your pension can cost you just £720.

Pay £1,000 into a workplace or personal pension the usual way (relief at source or net pay) and, as a basic-rate taxpayer, you get income tax relief only: 20% of £1,000 = £200, so it costs £800 of take-home pay. With salary sacrifice you give up £1,000 of salary and your employer pays the £1,000 into your pension instead. That pay is never taxed and skips employee National Insurance too: £200 income tax + £80 NI (8% between £12,570 and £50,270 in 2026/27) = £280 saved, so your take-home drops by just £720. Your employer also saves 15% NI (£150), and some employers add it to your pension.

The catch: from 6 April 2029 (the 2029-30 tax year), the National Insurance break is capped at £2,000 of salary sacrificed into a pension a year. Swap under £2,000 a year and nothing changes; above it, employee and employer NI are due on the extra (e.g. swap £3,000 and NI is due on £1,000: £80 for a basic-rate employee). It stays free of income tax. Higher-rate taxpayers save 40% tax + 2% NI, so £1,000 costs them about £580 today.

Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-thresholds-for-employers-2026-to-2027 · https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/pensions-tax-manual/ptm044220 · https://www.gov.uk/workplace-pensions/what-you-your-employer-and-the-government-pay · https://www.gov.uk/guidance/salary-sacrifice-and-the-effects-on-paye · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-salary-sacrifice-for-pensions-from-april-2029/changes-to-salary-sacrifice-for-pensions-from-april-2029 · https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2026/15

Illustration only. Assumes a basic-rate taxpayer in England, Wales or Northern Ireland earning between £12,570 and £50,270 (e.g. £35,000), whose employer offers salary sacrifice and pays the whole amount in. Salary sacrifice is your employer's choice to offer, can't take pay below the National Minimum Wage, and lowers the pay that some things are based on (such as statutory maternity pay and some earnings-related benefits). Scottish income tax bands differ. Rules as at 25 October 2026; the Budget on 28 October 2026 could change them. General education, not financial advice.
